deep.reconstruction:
SETTING (my inference from the previous folio, which works with A+iB, x+iy and divisibility by 1+i). The page belongs to Gauss's work on biquadratic residues. Here p = a^2 + b^2, with a odd, b even and gcd(a,b) = 1. Square brackets [x] denote the integer part (floor). The header says: t runs through all integers 1, 2, ..., b/2. All sums Σ below are over t = 1..b/2. Several sums written without brackets on the page are clearly meant as floor sums; this follows from the algebra.

Top-right marginalia: '½b+1−t' and 'b+2−2t' are reindexing aids. Under t -> b/2+1−t we get 2t−1 -> 2(b/2+1−t)−1 = b+1−2t.

(A) The function φ. Gauss uses φ(2b,c) = Σ_{s=1}^{b} [sc/(2b)], split into odd s = 2t−1 and even s = 2t:
φ(2b,b−a) = Σ[(2t−1)(b−a)/(2b)] + Σ[t(b−a)/b].
The second numerator is t(b−a), or 2t(b−a)/2b; the overwritten '(t−1)' cannot be right, as small cases show.

Step 1. Reindex the first sum: Σ[(2t−1)(b−a)/2b] = Σ[(b+1−2t)(b−a)/2b].

Step 2. Write [t(b−a)/b] = t + [−at/b]. Since gcd(a,b) = 1 and t < b, at/b is not an integer, so [−at/b] = −[at/b] − 1. Hence
Σ[t(b−a)/b] = Σt − Σ[at/b] − b/2.
The correct constant is Σt − b/2 = b(b+2)/8 − b/2 = b²/8 − b/4. Gauss writes '½b·½b+…' and then '+¼bb', i.e. he doubles Σt (see errors).

Step 3. The margin computation: (b+1−2t)(b−a) = (2t−1)a − (2t−1)b + b(b−a) = (2t−1)a − (2t−1+a−b)b.
Here 2t−1+a−b = 2t + (a−1−b) is even. So
[(b+1−2t)(b−a)/2b] = [(2t−1)a/2b] − (t + (a−1−b)/2).

Step 4. Sum over t. We have Σ(t + (a−1−b)/2) = b(b+2)/8 + (a−1−b)b/4. Gauss writes ¼(bb+2b) and ¼(a−1−b)b. All constants combine to
φ(2b,b−a) = Σ[(2t−1)a/2b] − Σ[at/b] − ¼(a+1−b)b.
This final identity is correct.

Step 5. He also defines Φ(2b,a) = Σ[(2t−1)a/2b] + Σ[at/b] = Σ_{s=1}^{b}[sa/2b].

(B) The quantity M. He records
M = (p−1)/8 + b/2 − ab/4 + 2·S1, where S1 = Σ[(2t−1)a/2b].
Presumably M is an exponent of i in a biquadratic character obtained by a Gauss-lemma count. Its exact meaning cannot be read off this page.

Step 6. Split odd from all: S1 = Σ[ta/2b] + Σ[(b/2+t)a/2b] − Σ[2ta/2b]. Here the first two sums together are Σ_{s=1}^{b}[sa/2b].

Step 7. Use [x] + [x+½] = [2x] with x = ta/2b: [ta/2b] − [ta/b] = −[(ta+b)/2b].

Step 8. Reindex t -> b/2+1−t: Σ[(b/2+t)a/2b] = Σ[(b+1−t)a/2b].

Step 9. Shift the index by one. This gains the u = 0 term [a/2] = (a−1)/2 and loses the u = b/2 term [a/4]:
Σ[(b+1−t)a/2b] = Σ[(b−t)a/2b] + (a−1)/2 − [a/4].

Step 10. Since a is odd, (b−t)a/2b = (a−1)/2 + (b−ta)/2b. Moreover [(b−ta)/2b] = −[(ta+b)/2b], because 2b does not divide ta−b. So
Σ[(b−t)a/2b] = b(a−1)/4 − Σ[(ta+b)/2b].
Therefore S1 = −2Σ[(ta+b)/2b] + ¼b(a−1) + ½(a−1) − [a/4].

Step 11. Substituting:
M = (p−1)/8 + b/2 − ab/4 + ab/2 − b/2 + a − 1 − 2[a/4] − 4Σ[(ta+b)/2b].
Now a − 1 − 2[a/4] = (a−1)/2 if a ≡ 1 (mod 4), and (a+1)/2 if a ≡ 3 (mod 4). Hence
M = (p−1)/8 + ab/4 + ½(a∓1) − 4Σ_{t=1}^{b/2}[(ta+b)/2b].

The point (my inference): the floor-sum term is a multiple of 4. So mod 4, M ≡ (p−1)/8 + ab/4 + (a∓1)/2. This is a closed form free of lattice-point counting, as needed for a supplementary law of biquadratic reciprocity.
errors: The constant from Σt is handled with a factor 2 error. Σ_{t=1}^{b/2} t = b(b+2)/8, but Gauss effectively uses b(b+2)/4. This shows in '½b·½b+…', in the line 'φ = … − Σ[at/b] + ¼bb', and in '+¼bb − ¼(bb+2b)'. Line 3 as written is therefore wrong: the true constant is b²/8 − b/4, not b²/4. The doubled term appears with opposite signs in both places, so it cancels. The net constant −b/2 − ¼(a−1−b)b = −¼(a+1−b)b is correct, and the final φ-identity holds.

Notational slip: several sums are written without floor brackets (e.g. Σ(b+1−2t)(b−a)/2b, Σ(2t−1)a/2b, Σ(ta+b)/2b, Σ(b+1−t)a/2b) although floor sums are meant. Read literally as rational sums, the identities would be false.

The second sum in the definition of φ(2b,b−a) appears as '(t−1)(b−a)/b' because of an overwrite. Only t(b−a)/b (= 2t(b−a)/2b) makes the identity true. For example, with a=1, b=4 the (t−1) reading gives φ=1, while the right-hand side gives 2.
The steps silently use gcd(a,b)=1, a odd, b even. These are needed for [−at/b] = −[at/b] − 1 and [(b−ta)/2b] = −[(ta+b)/2b]. This is legitimate in context (p = a²+b² prime) but unstated.
Apart from these, every step (Hermite duplication, reindexings, boundary terms [a/2] and [a/4], the case split giving ½(a∓1)) checks out.

results.what: Reduction of the full floor sum φ(2b,b−a) = Σ_{s=1}^{b}[s(b−a)/2b] to sums in a: φ(2b,b−a) = Σ_{t≤b/2}[(2t−1)a/2b] − Σ_{t≤b/2}[at/b] − ¼(a+1−b)b
results.modern_name: Elementary floor-function (lattice-point) sum manipulation, as in Eisenstein-style proofs of reciprocity via Gauss's lemma
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (lemma, 1808), Eisenstein (geometric lattice-point form, 1844); routine technique

results.what: Use of [x]+[x+1/2]=[2x] to convert Σ[ta/2b] − Σ[ta/b] into −Σ[(ta+b)/2b]
results.usually_credited_to: Hermite (general form, 1884); duplication case folklore, used by Gauss

results.what: Closed form of a Gauss-lemma-type exponent M for p=a²+b²: M = (p−1)/8 + ab/4 + ½(a∓1) − 4Σ_{t=1}^{b/2}[(ta+b)/2b], hence M ≡ (p−1)/8 + ab/4 + (a∓1)/2 (mod 4) for a ≡ ±1 (mod 4)
results.modern_name: Evaluation of a biquadratic residue character by lattice-point counting (supplementary laws of quartic reciprocity, e.g. for 2 or 1+i)
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (character of 2 and 1+i, Theoria residuorum biquadraticorum 1828/1832, plus Nachlass); lattice-point proofs by Eisenstein (1844)

deep.surprise_reason: This is working material for Gauss's own biquadratic theory, where he is already credited with the supplementary laws. Similar Gauss-lemma/floor-sum computations survive in his Nachlass (Werke II, X). The page is a careful but standard manipulation of floor sums. It adds a detail of method, close to Eisenstein's later lattice-point style, rather than a new result.

transcription_corrections: In the definition of φ(2b,b−a), the second sum should read Σ[t(b−a)/b] (possibly written 2t(b−a)/2b and overwritten), not Σ[(t−1)(b−a)/b].
Line 2 ends '½b·½b+…' (incomplete). It is Gauss's (doubled) value of Σt, presumably ½b(½b+1).
In 'Σ(b+1−2t)(b−a)/2b' and the later unbracketed sums, the intended meaning is a floor sum [ ]; Gauss omitted the brackets.
In 'Φ(2b,a) = Σ(2t−1)a/2b + Σ|at/b', read Σ[(2t−1)a/2b] + Σ[at/b].
In the split line, the subtracted sum read as 'Σ|at/2b]' is Σ[2at/2b] (= Σ[at/b]). The image shows a fraction over 2b.
Top-right marginalia '½b+1−t' and 'b+2−2t' are reindexing notes (2(½b+1−t) = b+2−2t, so 2t−1 -> b+1−2t). '43 of 28' is a struck-out archival number.
